new_statements.quote: According to this principle, if some elements enter in a two-way contrast, it is recommended that only one is represented graphically. Consequently, redundant (always predictable) marks can be omitted from the orthography. This principle explains why only the high toneme is marked graphically in all Gbe languages in the GUSO conventions; syllables without tone marks will generally be assigned the low toneme. [p. 75:] The Gbe lects known to us amount to about sixty. They are, in alphabetical order ...: ... Gen, Gun, Gbekon, Gbesi, Gbokpa, ...

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: statement check: group-level-statement. Capo's sentence is about GUSO conventions for 'all Gbe languages' (high toneme marked, low unmarked); Gbesi figures only as a name in the p.75 inventory of c. sixty lects. No Gbesi data or Gbesi-specific claim. | checker: Book confirmed by SUDOC SRU (Capo, 'The new ewe orthography', 2000, Cape Town/Garome: CASAS, ISBN 1-919799-36-2); archive.org itself was unreachable from this IP during my session (connection timeouts), but A's saved text is held by the project and I read it. Quote found verbatim at lines 4154-4171 of sec. 5.3 'Principle of economy', running heads pp. 87-88) and the lect inventory incl. 'Gbesi, Gbokpa' at line 3520 (sec. 3.2, p. 75).…
new_statements.relation_note: Gbe-wide: two tonemes (H marked, L unmarked); syllable structures V, CV, ClV, CyV (+nasal); no stress/accent statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: All Gbe lects (Gbesi and Gbokpa explicitly enumerated among them) are treated as having a two-way tonemic contrast, high vs low toneme, with only the high toneme. nothing is said about word stress or accent anywhere in the book ('stress' occurs only as the English verb).
new_statements.exceptions: High toneme 'descriptively has some variants such as the rising, the mid, etc.' (p. 8, for Ewe); first syllable of a reduplication read on the register of the second (p. 8-9). No lect-specific remarks for Gbesi.
new_statements.identity_note: A pan-Gbe orthography manual by the author of the Comparative Phonology of Gbe; sec. 3.2 (p. 75) enumerates the ~60 Gbe lects GUSO is designed for, explicitly including 'Gbesi, Gbokpa' (the two dialects of gbes1238). The tone statement is made for 'all Gbe languages', i.e. family-level, not a Gbesi-specific description. | PHOIBLE ties inventory 1282 to glottocode gbes1238 / ISO gbs by name 'gbesi'; the GM (African inventories) series extracted per-lect inventories from Capo 1991 ch. 2, whose Phla-Phera sample includes 'Gbesi lects' (Capo 1991 p. 14). Secondhand extraction, not Capo's prose.

sources.note: No phonology of Gbesi: only residual noun-class prefix vowels (Gbesi, Gbokpa: o- o- a- a- a-, '2' prefix types, Gun subgroup) and the remark that their Gun-like character reflects Whydah/Fon influence. Tone mentioned only for individual Gbe etyma elsewhere in the chapter (e.g. 'low-toned form /we/'), never for Gbesi; no stress statement.

sources.citation: Kluge, Angela. 2011. A sociolinguistic survey of the Gbe language communities of Benin and Togo: Gbe language family overview. SIL Electronic Survey Report 2011-012. 21 pp.
sources.note: Nothing. Classification only: Gbesi/Gbokpa group lexically with western Phla-Phera, grammatically with the Fon cluster (p. 8); fn. 13: Gbesi absent from Capo's (1986:101) classification but marked Phla-Phera on his map.

sources.note: Nothing. Sociolinguistic survey (comprehension testing, vitality, attitudes). Sec. 3 'Previous linguistic research' (p. 5-6) states the only prior work on Gbesi is Capo's comparative Gbe phonology and SIL/CNL word lists; sec. 6.1 (p. 10) notes only 'minor differences in tone' between villages.
